key_gap: Both sides produced the identical schedule — six sessions on days 0, 2, 6, 14, 30, 70 (gaps 2, 4, 8, 16, 40) — with identical retention arithmetic at both dates (massed 0 / 0.99, min ≈ 0; fixed-weekly 0.94 / 0.40, min ≈ 0.40; expanding 0.77 / 0.58, min ≈ 0.58) and the same max-min criterion over the two binding checkpoints. The gap is ordering and ownership: the human computed all three schedules from the decay curve and committed to the expanding shape in one first-pass move, owning the mechanism ('review while the half-life is small, double the gap as it doubles, place the last review as late as the earlier deadline allows — the exam is decided by the final review's placement, not the first') and the single-date subtlety (if only the exam bound, late fixed spacing would rival expanding; the growing gap is what serves two dates with six sessions). The AI reached the identical structure by generating and verifying the full alternative set inside its HOW stage before the pattern was obvious, stated the same insights later and more derivatively, and added packet-level uncertainty handling (h-estimate risk, skip rule, worst-case-is-B) the human did not bother with.
learning_signal: For scheduling problems with a given decay model, the retention math IS the method and should be the first move: (1) fix the model and enumerate the schedules' exposures, then compute expected retention at EVERY binding deadline from the curve (s = 0.5^(d/h), h growing per exposure) before any preference; (2) choose the criterion explicitly: when multiple dates bind, maximize the minimum (max-min), never the single-date optimum — a plan that zeros a binding checkpoint is not a schedule; (3) use the mechanism, not the label: expanding gaps are optimal because early reviews are cheap (steep decay, small h), gaps can grow as h doubles, and the final review's placement — not the first's — dominates the last deadline; (4) state the subtlety: if only the final date mattered, equal spacing with a late last review would rival expanding — the growing gap earns its keep exactly when multiple dates bind under a fixed session count; (5) make the schedule executable: coverage per session, hardest items in the largest-h sessions, and a skip rule (bring the next review forward) because the schedule is a contract, not a prophecy.
suggested_improvement: Add a 'schedule-first' pre-pass to HOW for time-placement problems with a given model: (a) before generating alternatives, compute each candidate schedule's expected outcome at every binding deadline directly from the given model and let max-min over the deadlines pick the winner; (b) treat 'compute retention per candidate' as the first verification pass, not a post-hoc check; (c) require a 'last-review placement' line and a 'binding-deadline minimum' line in the decision packet for every schedule recommendation; (d) add a skip-recovery rule (bring the next review forward) to packets that emit schedules.

key_gap: The pure style executed its own machinery flawlessly and failed on it: it itemized the platform docs into 500 cards, ran the expanding schedule (1-2-4-7-14-30) at ~28 of 30 hours of budget, and produced day-21 recall ~90% — with zero transfer: the engineer still could not trace a payment request end-to-end, which the scenario's own data says is the only thing that predicts first-bug-fix readiness. The bottleneck was first-pass comprehension (encoding), not decay (retention): nothing had been understood yet, so there was nothing for the schedule to protect, and the overhead (12h production + 16h reviews) left ~2h for the real task. The AI performed the bottleneck diagnosis instead: a 1-hour trace probe as the discriminating test, a partition of the material into fact-like items (SRS-eligible: endpoint names, flags, codes) vs understanding (not decomposable into cards — recall of isolated pieces does not compose into a money-flow model), and a comprehension-first plan (~10h spine: dependency-order reading, one end-to-end trace, a 2-page money-flow note, explain-back) with ~20h on a real end-to-end bug and SRS admitted only as a ≤30-min/day carve-out for residual facts from the leftover budget, with transfer — not recall — as the success metric.
learning_signal: The failure mode is SRS theater — running a perfect expanding schedule on a comprehension bottleneck: retention engineering optimizes what is retained, not what is understood. The core skill is the bottleneck probe + partition: (1) before scheduling anything, run a cheap discriminating probe that distinguishes encoding-failure ('can you apply/trace/use it today?') from decay ('understood, but weakening'); (2) partition the material into fact-like items (SRS-eligible: names, flags, codes) vs understanding (not decomposable — recall of isolated cards does not compose into a mental model); (3) when comprehension is the bottleneck, the spine is comprehension-first — dependency-order reading, one end-to-end trace, an explain-back — and SRS is admitted only for residual facts AFTER the model exists, from the leftover budget; (4) price the overhead explicitly: if the schedule consumes most of the budget while the binding activity gets ~0 hours, the schedule IS the cost; (5) tie the plan to the transfer metric (apply/trace/do), not to recall — if recall does not predict the goal, a recall plan cannot be the plan.
suggested_improvement: Add a 'bottleneck probe + partition' gate to the WHY stage for learning-plan tasks: (a) before approving any schedule, require a one-hour probe that tests the predictor skill (trace/apply/use) and an explicit answer to 'is the failure decay or first-encoding?'; (b) require the material to be partitioned into fact-like items vs understanding, and block card production for anything not yet understood — transcription is not encoding; (c) add an overhead line to the alternatives table: hours consumed by the schedule vs hours left for the binding activity; (d) require the plan's success metric to be the transfer metric the goal is measured on.
